headline: New moon springs load up Plum Gut as porgies stack thick around Shelter Island
subhead: Bass and blues are riding the building current through the Gut while fluke slide into the channels ahead of the weekend's big tides.
body_markdown:
Last week the bay did what it does in early July — it settled into that thick, green, warm-water rhythm that pushes everything toward structure and current. We had a stretch of light southwest wind that let the surface really cook, and with Great South Bay reportedly pushing 78.8 degrees, I'd bet dollars to donuts the shallow flats up here in Noyack and Southold Bay aren't far behind. That kind of heat doesn't ruin the fishing, it just relocates it. Bass, blues and fluke all read water temperature the same way we read a thermostat that's stuck too high — they go find the vent. Around here that means the channels, the Gut, and anywhere current keeps moving cooler water across structure.

This week the moon's swinging toward new, and that matters more in the Peconic system than almost anywhere else on the Island because Plum Gut and the Race live and die by tidal current. Springs build hard Friday through Monday (July 10-13), with peak exchange lining up right around the weekend. Bigger tides mean stronger current through the Gut, Shelter Island Sound, and the cuts around Jessups Neck and Robins Island — and stronger current means bait gets pushed off the flats and concentrated where predators can pin it. If you've been struggling to find fish scattered on the flats, this is the week that current does the work for you and stacks them up in the pinch points.

Porgy fishing has been the one constant, and honestly it's been about as good as it gets. I've been working the rockpiles off Cedar Point, the drop-off outside Fresh Pond, and the rips along the North Ferry side of Shelter Island in 15 to 25 feet, and it's been steady meat right through the tide changes — doesn't seem to matter if it's incoming or outgoing, though the bite does sharpen up in that hour before and after the turn when the current eases and the fish stop fighting to hold position. Standard hi-lo rig, size 6 or 4 hooks, fresh sandworm or a chunk of clam, just enough weight to hold bottom. Nothing fancy needed. These porgies are thick and eager, running 10 to 13 inches with enough 14s mixed in to keep it interesting, and there's no shortage of them right now — this is peak season for a reason.

Fluke have been the trickier read. Bay water warming the way it has pushed a chunk of the population out of the open flats and into the channels — the same pattern we're seeing bayside across the Island, just playing out on our geography. I'm finding better numbers working the Orient Point rip, the North Race, and the deeper cut running along Long Beach Bar in 20 to 35 feet on the outgoing tide, dragging a white Gulp Swimming Mullet on a half-ounce bucktail nice and slow along bottom. It's not been a banzai bite — more a fish here, a fish there, cull through some shorts to find a couple of keepers in the 18 to 20-inch range. If you want a shot at something bigger, work the deeper edge of the channel where it meets the flat, right where the thermocline sets up. That temperature break is holding bait, and bigger fluke sit right on that seam waiting on it.

Stripers have been a mixed bag, which is normal for mid-July in the bay system. The early-morning bite off the Shelter Island rips and around Orient Point has produced schoolies to the mid-20s mixed with the occasional bass pushing 30 inches, mostly on bucktails and swimming plugs worked through the faster water at first light before the sun gets up on it. Bluefish have actually been the more consistent player through Plum Gut itself — anywhere from cocktail-size choppers up to some solid 4 and 5-pounders blitzing bunker pods on the surface, especially on the stronger stages of the tide. Diamond jigs, poppers, anything flashy thrown into the melee gets hit. With the new moon building current through the Gut this weekend, I expect that bluefish action to sharpen up, and there's a real chance some better bass slide in behind the bait as the current rips harder and pins everything against the rocks off Orient.

Weakfish, I'll be honest, are still a no-show. Water's plenty warm enough on paper, but warm water alone isn't the trigger — I haven't heard of a legitimate weakfish catch in the bay in weeks, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise. If you're set on weakies, I'd hold off until we see some real reports rather than burning gas on a hunch.

Looking ahead, the building spring tide through the weekend is the headline event for this zone. If the wind stays out of the south and light like it has been, I'd fish the Gut and the North Race on the max ebb Saturday and Sunday morning — that's when the current will be moving the most water and stacking bait against structure. Bring bucktails for bass, diamond jigs for the blues, and don't leave the porgy rig at home, because Shelter Island's rockpiles aren't going anywhere and they'll bail you out if the current fishing goes quiet. Plan B if the Gut gets too ripping to fish comfortably: back off into Shelter Island Sound and work the porgies and fluke on the slower water while you wait for the tide to ease. Either way, there's enough happening in this system right now to make the trip worth it — just go in with a game plan for more than one species.
